questions.prompt: A commit that broke checkout is already on main, and five teammates have pulled it. What is the safest way to undo it?
options: git reset --hard HEAD~1, then git push --force to main
git revert <sha>, then push the new undo commit normally
git rebase -i to drop the commit, then force-push main
git stash the change, then git push to overwrite main
questions.explanation: Revert adds a new commit that cancels the old one, so shared history only grows and nobody's clone breaks. Reset and rebase rewrite published history and need a force-push.

questions.prompt: You rebased your personal feature branch onto the latest main. Now git push is rejected. What should you run?
options: git push --force-with-lease, which fails if the remote moved
git pull, then push again, to merge the old copies back in
git push --force, which is the same as --force-with-lease
git merge origin/feature, then push the merge commit
questions.explanation: Rebasing gave your commits new hashes, so a force-push is required. --force-with-lease refuses if someone else pushed since your last fetch, unlike plain --force; pulling would re-merge the old commits.

questions.prompt: After a botched git reset --hard, the commit 'add search' seems gone from your branch. What recovers it?
options: git stash pop restores the commits removed by the reset
Nothing can, because --hard deletes commits permanently
git revert HEAD brings back the commits the reset removed
git reflog to find its entry, then git branch rescue <entry>
questions.explanation: Reset only moved the branch pointer; the commit still exists and reflog records where HEAD was. Creating a branch at that entry brings it back. Only uncommitted changes are truly lost.

questions.prompt: Your Dockerfile runs COPY . . before RUN pip install -r requirements.txt. Every one-line code change triggers a 3-minute rebuild. What fixes it?
options: Switch the base image to python:latest so builds are faster
Copy requirements.txt and install first, then COPY . . last
Combine every instruction into a single long RUN command
Add EXPOSE 8000 so Docker knows which layers to cache
questions.explanation: A changed layer invalidates every layer after it. Installing dependencies before copying the source keeps the slow pip layer cached when only code changes.

questions.prompt: You run docker run -d -p 8080:8000 shop:1.0, but localhost:8080 refuses connections. The app logs 'listening on 127.0.0.1:8000'. Why?
options: Port 8080 must also be declared with EXPOSE in the Dockerfile
The -d flag hides the container's ports until it is attached
Inside the container the app must listen on 0.0.0.0, not loopback
The image name needs the latest tag for ports to be published
questions.explanation: 127.0.0.1 inside the container is the container's own loopback, which the port mapping cannot reach. Binding to 0.0.0.0 accepts traffic forwarded from the host. EXPOSE is documentation only.

questions.prompt: Production and staging both run shop:latest but behave differently. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: latest is a movable tag, so pin a version tag or a digest
latest images always pull from a different registry each time
Containers share kernels, so switch both to virtual machines
The image layers expired, so rebuild with docker commit
questions.explanation: latest is just a default tag name that can point to different images on different hosts or at different times. Pinning a version, or better a sha256 digest, guarantees the same image everywhere.

questions.prompt: In Compose, your web service fails with 'connection refused' to localhost:6379, where Redis should be. The Redis service is named cache. What do you change?
options: Publish Redis on the host with ports: ["6379:6379"] instead
Connect to cache:6379, since services resolve each other by name
Add network_mode: host to every service in compose.yaml
Move both processes into a single container to share localhost
questions.explanation: Each container has its own localhost. Compose puts services on a shared network where the service name, cache, resolves through Docker DNS to the Redis container.

questions.prompt: web starts before Postgres accepts connections and crashes, even though it has depends_on: [db]. What is the proper fix?
options: Add restart: always to db so it starts up faster than web
List db before web in compose.yaml so it is created first
Give db a healthcheck and use condition: service_healthy
Replace depends_on with links: [db] for strict ordering
questions.explanation: Plain depends_on only orders container start, not readiness. A healthcheck such as pg_isready plus condition: service_healthy makes web wait until the database answers.

questions.prompt: A teammate runs docker compose down -v to 'reset the network' and loses the local database. Why?
options: -v also deletes named volumes, which hold the database files
-v rebuilds every image from scratch, without the data layer
-v switches Compose into verbose mode, which wipes the caches
-v removes the .env file, so the database password is lost
questions.explanation: down removes containers and networks but keeps volumes; -v also deletes named volumes, where the database stored its data. Plain down, or restart, would have been enough.

questions.prompt: A node running 2 of your Deployment's 3 Pods loses power. What brings the count back to 3?
options: The kubelet on the dead node restarts the Pods once power returns
Nothing happens until an engineer runs kubectl scale again
etcd copies the two Pods' containers onto the nearest node
The ReplicaSet controller sees too few Pods and creates new ones
questions.explanation: Controllers continuously compare desired state (replicas: 3) with actual state. The ReplicaSet controller creates replacements and the scheduler places them on healthy nodes.

questions.prompt: Pods keep getting new IP addresses as they restart. Other apps in the cluster need one stable address for them. What do you create?
options: A ClusterIP Service selecting the Pods by their label
A NodePort on port 80, edited each time a Pod restarts
A second namespace that pins the Pod IP addresses
A bare Pod with a fixed IP address set in its YAML
questions.explanation: A Service gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name and load-balances to whichever ready Pods match its selector. ClusterIP is the default type and is internal to the cluster.

questions.prompt: kubectl apply rejects your new Deployment. Its selector says app: web, but the Pod template is labeled app: api. What is wrong?
options: The scheduler cannot find a node with enough CPU for app: api
The selector must match the template's labels, so they need to agree
Deployments need a Service before they can create any Pods
Labels only work inside the default namespace, not custom ones
questions.explanation: A Deployment manages the Pods its selector matches, so the template labels must satisfy the selector. The API server rejects a mismatch; make the two agree, ideally with a stable label.

questions.prompt: During a database blip, all Pods of your API restart at once and the outage gets longer. Their liveness probe calls the database. What should change?
options: Raise memory limits so the Pods can survive the restart
Check the database in readiness only; keep liveness local
Remove the readiness probe and keep the liveness probe
Scale to more replicas so some Pods skip the liveness check
questions.explanation: Failing liveness restarts containers, so a shared dependency failure restarts everything. Readiness only removes Pods from traffic, which is the right reaction to a dependency outage.

questions.prompt: A Pod shows CrashLoopBackOff and describe reports Last State: Terminated, Exit Code 137, Reason OOMKilled. What is the best first fix?
options: Raise the memory limit or reduce the app's memory usage
Add more CPU to the request so the app runs faster
Delete the Pod so a fresh one starts without a backoff
Recreate the Secret, since 137 means a missing key
questions.explanation: 137 is SIGKILL, and OOMKilled means the container exceeded its memory limit. Deleting the Pod just repeats the crash; raise the limit (and request) or fix the memory usage.

questions.prompt: An HPA targets 70% CPU. There are 4 replicas averaging 105% of their CPU request. How many replicas does it aim for (min 2, max 10)?
options: 5 replicas
8 replicas
6 replicas
10 replicas
questions.explanation: desired = ceil(4 x 105 / 70) = ceil(6.0) = 6, which is within the 2-10 bounds. Utilization is measured against requests, so the Pods need CPU requests.
